sessions.title: Twelve Messages
sessions.summary: Everything typed to take a live event from spreadsheet chaos to published social content — and the method that made the other 99% happen.
sessions.audience: Anyone delegating real work to an AI agent — functional through deeply technical.
sessions.evidence: The verbatim conversation, a five-principle method, the pipeline that runs it, and two honest failures.
sessions.practice: Steal the shape: templates over outputs, constraints in the repo, judgment kept human.

artifact.alt: Published Instagram story rendered by the demo's pipeline

sessions.title: The Browser Is a Shell Command
sessions.summary: Replacing 18,000 tokens of always-loaded browser-automation schema with ten shell commands and a README — and why the agent gets sharper, not weaker.
sessions.audience: Agent users paying token tax for tools they barely touch; builders choosing between MCP and CLIs.
sessions.evidence: The cost math, four design choices that make a tool agent-friendly, live transcripts, and where MCP still wins.
sessions.practice: Audit your always-loaded schemas, then wrap the five operations you actually use as small composable commands.

artifact.alt: Demo 02 title slide: the browser is a shell command, with a real browse-shot transcript

sessions.title: Taught Once, Enforced Forever
sessions.summary: Corrections given in chat decay when the session ends. The fix is changing the agent's environment — helpers, deny-hooks, and CI ratchets that carry the rule forever.
sessions.audience: Anyone tired of re-teaching their agent the same rule every session.
sessions.evidence: Four real guards with their origin audits, verbatim deny messages, and the five properties that keep guardrails from getting ripped out.
sessions.practice: Count your repeated corrections, then promote them up the ladder: wrapper, hook, CI gate — stopping at the lowest level that holds.

artifact.alt: Demo 03 title slide, featuring a real read-guard denial of an oversized screenshot

sessions.title: Your Sessions Are a Corpus
sessions.summary: A 24 GB session archive forced the next question: how do you keep the lessons, prove closeout, and let the raw record expire?
sessions.audience: Anyone who has corrected an AI twice and watched the correction evaporate with the session.
sessions.evidence: The mining loop end to end, plus the measured retention incident that separated canonical truth, compact recall, raw transcripts, and reproducible worktree output.
sessions.practice: Close one session into an outcome, evidence, open questions, and next action before deciding whether its raw transcript is safe to expire.

artifact.alt: Demo 04 title slide: a real artifact-miner run over 2,747 transcripts

sessions.title: The Product That Files Its Own Tickets
sessions.summary: End users file feedback, an LLM judge triages it into GitHub Issues, an agent implements the safe ones — with the autonomy boundary in deterministic code and a human holding the only merge key.
sessions.audience: Anyone deciding how much of an incoming-work queue to hand to an agent.
sessions.evidence: The four-stage loop, the allowlist gate read from live source, six real tickets sorted by lane, and a run ledger whose best result was declining to fabricate a fix.
sessions.practice: Let the model classify, never authorize: write the autonomy boundary as a small tested allowlist, and keep merging human.

artifact.alt: Demo 05 title slide with a real agent-lane ticket and its labels

sessions.title: The Registry of Landmines
sessions.summary: Some load-bearing facts are invisible to search — the code compiles and the behavior is still wrong. One registry file holds them, a derive catalog enforces them in CI, and a meta-test keeps the registry from lying about itself.
sessions.audience: Anyone whose agent (or teammate) keeps re-learning the same expensive lesson.
sessions.evidence: The bug that shipped twice, the token economics of pre-paid conclusions, the why/decided/currently-true split, and the registry-about-the-registry.
sessions.practice: Start the file the second time something breaks for the same reason; derive the status, never hand-edit it.

artifact.alt: Demo 06 title slide with the shipped-twice landmine exhibit

sessions.title: The Agent Said It Checked
sessions.summary: "Verified" is a sentence, not a fact. A security migration passed its audit while production was broken — and the discipline that came out of it caught three more false claims building this very series.
sessions.audience: Anyone who has accepted an AI's (or a doc's, or their own) claim that something was checked.
sessions.evidence: The circular-audit failure mode, a prod-broke-twice case study peeled layer by layer, and the re-derivation discipline with its real budget.
sessions.practice: Ask "checked how?" — then run that check yourself: grep the file, run the command, end at the runtime.

artifact.alt: Demo 07 title slide with a claim-versus-runtime-check exhibit

sessions.title: Gates Between Agentic Stages
sessions.summary: Agents are strong inside a stage and unreliable at the boundaries. A delivery methodology built on that: deterministic gates between agentic stages — 88 versioned revisions, 14 running initiatives, and the day production published fiction.
sessions.audience: Anyone chaining AI work across stages — draft to review, analysis to deck, prototype to production.
sessions.evidence: The deterministic-core/agentic-shell shape, the migration-sweep incident and the inverted check it left behind, and a methodology versioned like a product.
sessions.practice: Make artifacts declare what they are; gate every hand-off mechanically; version your process with a changelog.

artifact.alt: Demo 08 title slide: the staged pipeline with gate posts between every stage

sessions.title: The Beautifier Was an Auditor
sessions.summary: A skill built to make a README prettier turned out to be a drift detector. Across five repos it flagged a deploy doc still pointing at a platform the project left months ago, a command list that no longer matched the actual commands, and capabilities the code had grown that nobody had written down. The visual polish was the smallest thing it did.
sessions.audience: Anyone about to run a 'polish' or 'cleanup' pass on their docs — and anyone who trusts a cosmetic tool to stay in its lane.
sessions.evidence: Why a beautifier's real payload is its inspect step, five repos' worth of drift it surfaced, and one honest failure — claiming checked when the check was only partial.
sessions.practice: Run the audit pass first: fix what's wrong before polishing what's already fine — and verify the render where it actually ships, not just locally.

artifact.alt: Demo 09 title slide: a README claim beside the code fact that contradicts it

sessions.title: The Chiropractor's Four Questions
sessions.summary: A sports chiropractor asked four plain questions about selling rehab programs from his website. The AI's answer was confident, tabulated, sourced — and its evidence was marketing all the way down. Twice.
sessions.audience: Anyone who asks an AI to research a real decision — especially when the answer goes to someone who can't check the work.
sessions.evidence: A first pass built on vendors ranking themselves, a 'correction' that swapped in a competitor's stat, three refuted claims with the fetches that killed them, and the confidence-label system that came out the other side.
sessions.practice: Ask "did you read the source, or a search result about it?" — then make the answer a visible label on every number that ships.

artifact.alt: Demo 10 title slide with a confidence tag being downgraded from verified to search-derived

sessions.title: The Sycophancy Was in the Config
sessions.summary: A rival model reviewing my agent's work looked sharper — it demanded competing candidates and restraint. So my agent A/B tested its own harness: same model, same prompt, config on and off. The vanilla arm pushed back on me twice. The configured arm never did.
sessions.audience: Anyone who compares AI tools and concludes one model is smarter — and anyone whose agent config has grown by accretion.
sessions.evidence: A twelve-run experiment on a live harness: the bare-mode control arm, a self-contaminating probe, a scorecard separating model habits from config damage, and one validated sentence that flipped the behavior 2/2.
sessions.practice: Before blaming the model, run the bare arm — then test candidate rules as experiment arms and promote only what the grid validates.

artifact.alt: Demo 11 title slide: the sycophancy was in the config, with the operator's verbatim question about model versus configuration

sessions.title: One Component I Didn't Already Have
sessions.summary: A plugin advertising eleven agents and fifty-four hooks, measured against the setup I already run. Of the eight components that could land on my machine, three were already going, one was the wrong platform, one was broken upstream, two were costs. The delta was one.
sessions.audience: Anyone handed a feature list and asked whether to adopt it — especially with a year of accumulated hooks, rules, and helpers already loaded.
sessions.evidence: A component-by-component subtraction against a real machine, three mechanical queries against the part of a repo nobody curates, a retracted recommendation, and the correction that produced all of it.
sessions.practice: Write your baseline down, sort the tool's list into native, new, and blocked, then search its tracker for the uninstall before you run the install.

artifact.alt: Demo 12 title slide: one component I didn't already have, with the operator's verbatim request to compare the tool against what he already runs

sessions.title: The Gate Was Written First
sessions.summary: Three ways to make a meeting archive answer a question, three preregistered gates, three refusals in one day. Each gate was committed to git before the model weights finished downloading — so when the scores came back plausible, there was nothing left to negotiate with. The feature that shipped is the one the evidence admitted.
sessions.audience: Anyone whose agent keeps wiring features that demo well and fail in use — and anyone deciding when a measured capability is allowed to become product.
sessions.evidence: A one-day trilogy of preregistered probes — a similarity floor, a pairwise scorer, an extractive no-answer head — each gate frozen before first inference, each failed without tuning; the falsifier showing a right answer scoring below a wrong one, which no threshold can fix; and the honest feature that shipped instead.
sessions.practice: Commit fixture, model digests, thresholds, prediction, and consequences before the first run. Observe the held-out result once. When the gate fails, record the receipt and stop — the refusal is the deliverable.

artifact.alt: Demo 13 title slide: the gate was written first, with the preregistration commit that predates the model download

sessions.title: Kibble & Co. Doesn't Sell Anything
sessions.summary: A pet-supply storefront went live on a real BigCommerce sandbox, moving real Stripe-sandbox money through real dunning logic — and it exists only so a subscription-billing platform could be built against a genuine store instead of a slide deck. Five deployed apps, 94 ADRs, and a generated file that answers 'what's shipped' so nobody has to narrate it. The method is the point; the pet food is the test fixture.
sessions.audience: Anyone evaluating whether spec-driven, agent-orchestrated delivery produces real software, and anyone deciding whether 'proposal → synthesis → ADR' is process theater or a working discipline.
sessions.evidence: A five-app BigCommerce subscriptions platform — storefront, admin, API, docs, marketing — built against a live sandbox store behind a fictional pet-supply merchant; 94 ADRs and 218 user stories moving through one repo; the mechanical state-derivation file that replaces status narration; and two real failures, a circular verification audit and a GitHub rate-limit exhaustion, with the fixes that shipped.
sessions.practice: Route every spec edit through proposal → synthesis → ADR with the synthesis ID in the commit message. Make 'what's shipped' a generated file, never a written claim. Build a disposable, fictional storefront when you need real platform behavior without a real merchant's data on the line.

artifact.alt: Demo 14 title slide: Kibble & Co. doesn't sell anything, the fictional pet-supply storefront built to make subscription flows real

sessions.title: The Harder Deliverable Wasn't the Build
sessions.summary: A ten-document vendor bid package — the scoping and estimation kit a global systems integrator needs before it can bid on a BigCommerce-native subscriptions build — projected from a 28-epic, 218-story spec corpus in days, not weeks. A leakage lint hard-fails before a forbidden pattern ever reaches the export, and a bundling script freezes identical, name-stamped copies per vendor. Every document still carries status: draft-internal-review — the release checklist stayed a human's job.
sessions.audience: Anyone evaluating how a client-facing deliverable — a bid package, an SOW, a scoping document — can be produced by agents without becoming a liability the moment it reaches an outside reader.
sessions.evidence: How a 10-document, 28-epic, 218-story vendor bid package gets projected — not authored — from a canonical spec corpus, sanitized by a hard-fail leakage lint instead of a proofread, frozen into identical per-vendor bundles, and held behind an unchecked human release checklist before anything ships.
sessions.practice: Keep one canonical source and generate every client-facing artifact from it. Make leakage prevention a whitelist-based lint that runs before the file is written, not a review step someone can skip. Write the release checklist before the package exists.

artifact.alt: Demo 15 title slide: the harder deliverable wasn't the build, showing the ten-document bid package's document list and story counts

sessions.title: The Agent That Asks Twice
sessions.summary: Ask BC is a production agent with 29 tools against a live commerce store — 22 that read, 7 that can change it — deployed split across a Next.js app and a Cloudflare Worker with a Durable Object per store. Every mutation needs two turns: a preview, then an explicit confirm. Months later, a sibling platform copied the runtime wholesale for its own merchant copilot — same Durable Object, same codemode sandbox, same two-turn writes — and pointed it at a different API entirely.
sessions.audience: Anyone deciding how much autonomy to hand an agent that can mutate a real system, and anyone wondering whether an agent pattern built once actually gets reused, or just described as reusable.
sessions.evidence: The two-turn confirmation pattern read straight from the tool code — nothing mutates on the first call, only on an explicit second call with the confirm flag set to true; the generative-UI block protocol that turns tool output into an inline React component instead of a wall of markdown; the Haiku-default, Sonnet-on-retry model split; a real security gap caught and fixed a month before the app's custom domain went live; and the decision record where a second product adopted the identical Durable-Object-plus-codemode runtime for its own copilot, pointed at an entirely different data plane.
sessions.practice: Put the confirmation gate inside the tool's own execute function, keyed on an explicit boolean the model must set — not a line in the prompt. Route the cheap model by default and upgrade only the step that needs it. When a pattern proves itself once, let the next build copy the runtime and swap only the data plane.

artifact.alt: Demo 16 title slide: the agent that asks twice, showing the preview-then-execute turn card

sessions.title: The Layout Was Inferred, Not Designed
sessions.summary: Aisles is a headless storefront that decides its own layout per shopper — 31 weighted rules feed a Bayesian inference engine that picks one of four personas, then an AI model generates the category page from a four-component vocabulary a Zod schema won't let it leave. Same URL, same catalog, four schema-valid layouts. On 2026-08-12 it was pointed at a real BigCommerce store for the first time — a brand-config entry, two environment variables, a harvested palette with file-line citations, and one honest bug: a client-side lookup that silently rendered furniture navigation over a pet-supply catalog.
sessions.audience: Anyone evaluating whether AI-generated UI can be made safe to ship, and anyone deciding how much of a personalization engine should be inferred versus hand-coded per segment.
sessions.evidence: The full pipeline read from source — 31 rules, a gatherer-biased Bayesian prior, and a softmax over four named personas (gatherer, hunter, researcher, gifter); the Zod schema that makes an AI-written layout provably valid instead of usually reasonable; the per-persona prompt language that actually reaches the model; the same-day integration against a live BigCommerce sandbox that took one config file because the catalog seam was already generic; a palette harvested from the storefront's own CSS with file and line citations; and the client-side brand-resolution bug the integration surfaced, with its fix.
sessions.practice: Build one catalog function that reads the active brand's config instead of one function per brand. Pass a typed schema to the model as a generation constraint, not a suggestion in the prompt. Harvest brand colors from the real source with a citation, never invent them. When a config is read in both server and client code, make sure it resolves identically in both — the client's silent fallback is the bug that ships.

artifact.alt: Demo 17 title slide: the layout was inferred, not designed, with the four-persona quad — gatherer, hunter, researcher, gifter

sessions.title: The Guardrail Removed the Storefront
sessions.summary: I asked one agent to make an AI storefront look as good as the real one, then handed the work to a second agent in four words: “pick up where Claude ended.” Nineteen commits later the AI was gone — and every commit message was a safety word. Nobody typed “remove the model.” The tests stayed green because they were rewritten to expect it. What caught it was remembering what the live site used to do.
sessions.audience: Anyone running work across two agents, or across days, and anyone who has watched a reasonable safety concern quietly redefine what the product is.
sessions.evidence: The verbatim direction that started it and the four-word handoff that dropped it; 27 agent sessions in one repository in a day, zero containing a typed instruction — every operator turn an auto-generated approval; the nineteen-commit verb ladder, where no single commit is wrong and the sequence deletes the feature; the green status line reporting “zero model requests” as an achievement for a product built on model requests; the contract test rewritten from listing model-authorized zones to asserting there are none; and the second overshoot, where the agent sent to fix the mistake made it again first.
sessions.practice: Restate the goal in the first message to the second agent — the plan file carries the paths and drops the why. Review runs of commits, not single diffs; a ratchet is a sequence. Label every number as a fixture property or a product target before it goes green. Keep one test that costs money, so a suite cannot pass hardest when the feature is gone.

artifact.alt: Demo 18 title slide: the guardrail removed the storefront, with the four-step chain from direction to handoff to hardening to removal

techniques.title: Two Ways to Draw a System
techniques.summary: Hand-authored SVG vs themed Mermaid — chosen per diagram, both shown working.
techniques.description: How an AI agent draws a technical diagram that looks like your project and doesn't go stale — hand-authored SVG vs themed Mermaid, chosen per diagram. The first Applied technique companion to the ways-of-working session demos.
principles: Choose the diagram form instead of defaulting to one.
Make the visual system native to the project, not the tool.
Read the system before drawing it.

techniques.title: Mine Your Own Transcripts
techniques.summary: Treat your agent sessions as a searchable corpus — corrections become priors the next session reads.
techniques.description: Every agent session is a transcript you usually throw away. Mine them instead: reusable prompts, your corrections as standing priors, and counted waste numbers that justify the next fix. The loop, from 614 real sessions.
principles: Treat past sessions as your best reference.
Turn repeated corrections into priors the next session reads.
Re-derive important numbers when you use them.

techniques.title: Gate Every Hand-Off
techniques.summary: Agents work inside a stage; deterministic gates verify between. Gate the seam, not the middle.
techniques.description: An AI agent is strong inside a stage and weak at the seams between them. The fix is a deterministic gate on every hand-off — a non-AI check the agent can't talk its way past. The shape, and the day production published fiction.
principles: Keep agents inside stages and deterministic gates between them.
Derive the stage from disk instead of trusting the claim.
Do not mistake a second agent for a gate.

techniques.title: Promote a Correction to a Guardrail
techniques.summary: Wrapper → deny-hook → CI ratchet: promote a repeated correction to the lowest rung that holds.
techniques.description: A correction you give an AI in chat dies with the session. The fix is changing its environment — a wrapper, a deny-hook, or a CI ratchet — so the rule holds forever. The three-rung ladder, with real deny-hooks firing.
principles: Promote a correction on the second repeat, not the first.
Use the lowest enforcement rung that holds.
Ship every guardrail with an escape hatch.

techniques.title: A Registry for What Grep Can't Find
techniques.summary: Facts grep can't surface, held in one registry and enforced in CI — the conclusion, pre-paid once.
techniques.description: Some load-bearing facts are invisible to search — the code compiles and the behavior is still wrong. Hold them in one registry, enforce the mechanical ones in CI, and split why / decided / currently-true. The technique, quoted from a real 25-entry registry.
principles: Write the conclusion, not the search.
Trust test-backed facts and re-confirm verified-against claims.
Start the registry the second time the same hidden fact causes a failure.

techniques.title: Put Provenance Labels on AI Research
techniques.summary: Three label tiers, an adversarial re-derivation loop, and the honest downgrade — shown working.
techniques.description: How to make AI-assisted research trustworthy for a reader who can't check it: a three-tier confidence label on every number, an adversarial audit loop that re-derives claims at their sources, and the honest downgrade when a source can't be read. The technique behind demo 10.
principles: Distinguish a source you read from a search result about it.
Check who owns the domain behind every claim.
Prefer an honest downgrade to a false confirmation.

techniques.title: Bare-Arm Test Your Agent Config
techniques.summary: A control arm for your own harness: bare mode, isolation arms, and rules validated before adoption.
techniques.description: How to tell whether an AI behavior gap is the model or your harness: run the same model bare as a control arm, isolate suspect config blocks, validate candidate rules as experiment arms, and promote only what the grid confirms. The technique behind demo 11.
principles: Run the control arm before drawing conclusions.
Score behaviors, not vibes.
Pin the worktree and fence the reads.
Promote a rule only after the experiment validates it.

techniques.title: Run the Subtraction Before You Install
techniques.summary: A feature list is half a subtraction. Enumerate your baseline, sort the tool's list into three buckets, then search its tracker for the uninstall.
techniques.description: Four checks that run before anything touches your machine: enumerate what you already have, subtract it from what the tool ships into native, new, and blocked, query the part of the repository nobody curates, and confirm the uninstall actually works. The technique behind demo 12.
principles: A feature list is half a subtraction.
Sort the result into native, new, and blocked.
Treat the issue tracker as the half nobody curates.
Check the exit before the entrance.

techniques.title: Close the Session, Keep the Lesson
techniques.summary: Turn a finished agent session into durable project truth and compact recall before its raw transcript expires.
techniques.description: Promote project truth, distill the reusable method, enqueue fast, mine in the background, and delete raw transcripts only after an explicit archive-safety receipt.
principles: Project truth stays with the project that owns it.
Lifecycle hooks enqueue; background workers mine.
A current watermark proves ingestion, not semantic completeness.

techniques.title: One Heavy Job at a Time
techniques.summary: Local inference makes scheduling an operational decision — and a panic's exit reason is two published integers, not a guess.
techniques.description: Running a model locally turns a laptop into a machine that has to be scheduled. A kernel panic during an inference run, how to decode the panic's exit reason from the vendor's own header instead of guessing at it, and the habits that made recovery a twenty-minute job instead of a lost morning.
principles: Give a local model run the machine to itself.
Look the panic's namespace and subcode up in the vendor's header before translating them.
Write results atomically, into a directory the system is not allowed to wipe.

techniques.title: The Home AI Server Question
techniques.summary: A measured local-versus-frontier comparison, plus the cost inputs for deciding whether to buy a home AI server.
techniques.description: A measured local-versus-frontier comparison built from the Yawn note-taking study and a context-plane experiment. It separates model quality, privacy, latency, operating cost, and the hardware bill before asking whether a Mac mini or Mac Studio earns its place.
principles: Measure the workload before buying the machine.
Route private, repetitive work locally and reserve frontier calls for jobs that need them.
Count correction time and operating cost, not just API tokens.
Treat a failed comparison as useful evidence about the pipeline, not only the model.
